en: Petavatthu, Uragavagga 12. Uragapetavatthu The Story of the Snake-Preta Long ago, monks, there was a certain village headman who was wealthy, possessing great riches and vast means. He had abundant gold, silver, bullion, and property; much grain, wealth, and various commodities; many fields, lands, and estates; many wives, concubines, and female attendants; many male and female slaves, and many laborers and servants. He was devoted to the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. He was devoted to his parents, devoted to ascetics and brahmins, and devoted to the practice of giving alms. He was compassionate toward all living beings. Now, at that time, there was a certain snake-king named Uraga who lived in a hole near that village headman’s house. One day, while the village headman was sitting on the veranda of his house, he saw the snake-king Uraga crawling out from his hole. Seeing him, he thought: "This snake-king Uraga is a creature of great power and majesty. If I were to give this snake-king Uraga a portion of my food, it would be well done. Then, monks, the village headman took a portion of his own food and gave it to the snake-king Uraga. Having given it, he made this aspiration: "By this root of merit, may I become a wheel-turning monarch in this very same village. Monks, after the passing away of that village headman, he was reborn in a certain royal family. When he grew up, he was anointed as king and became a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success.

Monks, the snake-king Uraga, having passed away from that state, was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings. There, monks, the snake-king Uraga dwelt in the assembly of the Four Great Kings, enjoying the pleasures of the gods. At that time, monks, the Four Great Kings addressed the devas of Tāvatiṃsa: "Friends, there is a wheel-turning monarch in such-and-such a village who is righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. Come, friends, let us go to see that wheel-turning monarch. Then, monks, the devas of Tāvatiṃsa approached the Four Great Kings and said: "Sirs, we have heard that there is a wheel-turning monarch in such-and-such a village who is righteous... possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. We wish to go and see him. "Friends," said the Four Great Kings, "that wheel-turning monarch is a human being, and we are gods. It is not fitting for us to go to see a human being. A second time, a third time, the devas of Tāvatiṃsa requested the same thing, and the Four Great Kings replied the same way. Finally, monks, the Four Great Kings consented to the request of the devas of Tāvatiṃsa. Then, monks, the Four Great Kings, accompanied by a great host of devas, went to the village where the wheel-turning monarch resided. There, monks, the Four Great Kings stood at the gate of the village and sent a messenger to the wheel-turning monarch: "Sire, the Four Great Kings, accompanied by a great host of devas, stand at the village gate desiring to see you. Please grant them an audience. "Very well," said the wheel-turning monarch, and he granted them an audience. Then, monks, the Four Great Kings entered the village and sat down in the appointed place. The wheel-turning monarch also entered the village and sat down in the appointed place. As they sat together, monks, the Four Great Kings spoke to the wheel-turning monarch: "Sire, you are a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. You are indeed fortunate, sire, you are indeed blessed. Then, monks, the Four Great Kings rose from their seats, paid homage to the wheel-turning monarch, and departed. Monks, after the passing away of that wheel-turning monarch, he was reborn in a certain royal family. When he grew up, he was anointed as king and became a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. Monks, the snake-king Uraga, having passed away from that state, was reborn in the realm of the Thirty-three Gods. There, monks, the snake-king Uraga dwelt in the assembly of the Thirty-three Gods, enjoying the pleasures of the gods. At that time, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, addressed the devas of Tāvatiṃsa: "Friends, there is a wheel-turning monarch in such-and-such a village who is righteous... possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. Come, friends, let us go to see that wheel-turning monarch. Then, monks, the devas of Tāvatiṃsa approached Sakka, lord of the devas, and said: "Sire, we have heard that there is a wheel-turning monarch in such-and-such a village who is righteous... possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. We wish to go and see him. "Sirs," said Sakka, lord of the devas, "that wheel-turning monarch is a human being, and we are gods. It is not fitting for us to go to see a human being. A second time, a third time, the devas of Tāvatiṃsa requested the same thing, and Sakka, lord of the devas, replied the same way. Finally, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, consented to the request of the devas of Tāvatiṃsa. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, accompanied by a great host of devas, went to the village where the wheel-turning monarch resided. Please grant him an audience. "Very well," said the wheel-turning monarch, and he granted him an audience. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, entered the village and sat down in the appointed place. The wheel-turning monarch also entered the village and sat down in the appointed place. As they sat together, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, spoke to the wheel-turning monarch: "Sire, you are a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. You are indeed fortunate, sire, you are indeed blessed. Then, monks, Sakka, lord of the devas, rose from his seat, paid homage to the wheel-turning monarch, and departed. Monks, after the passing away of that wheel-turning monarch, he was reborn in a certain royal family. When he grew up, he was anointed as king and became a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a ruler of the world, a conqueror of the four quarters, who established stability in the land, possessing the seven treasures and the four kinds of success. Monks, the snake-king Uraga, having passed away from that state, was reborn in the realm of the Yāma Gods. There, monks, the snake-king Uraga dwelt in the assembly of the Yāma Gods, enjoying the pleasures of the gods.

Just as a snake casts off its worn-out skin and goes away,
so too [the wise man] leaves behind this useless body.
When one has passed away and died,
burning, one does not know the lamentation of one's kinsmen.
"Therefore, I do not weep for him;
he has gone to whatever destination is his.
"He has come back from there unafraid," [the mother said].
He did not depart from here without permission;
as he came, so he went.
What cause for lamentation is there in that?
Being consumed by fire, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore, I do not weep for him.
"He has gone to whatever destination belongs to him.
"If I were to weep, I would become emaciated;
what fruit would there be for me in that?"
There would be even greater displeasure toward kinsmen, friends, and companions.
One who is burning does not know [this].
The lamentation of relatives;
therefore, I do not weep for him,
for he has gone to whatever destination is his.
"Just as a child cries out after the moon as it moves away,
so too is this pursuit of worldly success."
Even one who grieves for the deceased, while burning with anguish,
does not perceive the lamentations of their kinsmen.
"Therefore, I do not weep for him;
he has gone to whatever destination is his.
"Just as, O Brahmā, a water-jar..."
They are separated and will not reconnect;
such is the nature of things,
yet he who grieves for the deceased does so in vain.
Burning, he does not know the lamentation of his kinsmen;
therefore, I do not weep for this.
"He has gone to whatever destination belongs to him.
The twelfth Uraga Petavatthu.
The first Uraga Chapter is concluded.
Its summary verse:
The field, the pig, the putrid,
the flour, and also through the wall.
The five [monks], Sattaputta, Goṇa, the weaver,
and likewise the elephant Khallāṭiya;
"And twelve snakes."
